Topic: If a starving man steals rice from a lord's granary to feed his child, does the theft weigh the same on the scale of virtue as if he had stolen it to feed his greed?
Austen — Judgement:
A theft is one entry in the magistrate's ledger, but I have never yet found a ledger that could weigh a motive — and motive is where I do my accounting.

Society is generous in excusing the vices of the comfortable and severe upon the necessities of the poor; a rich man's economy is called prudence, a poor man's identical act called meanness or crime. The father who steals rice to keep his child from starving obeys the first duty nature lays upon us — the preservation of those entrusted to our care. The man who steals from greed answers no duty at all; he merely enlarges an appetite already indulged past reason. To judge both by the act alone, and never by the necessity or the vanity behind it, is to mistake the letter of virtue for its living spirit.

The two thefts are identical in law and opposite in conscience.

*Necessity may excuse what greed can never justify — the statute counts one crime, but the heart always counts two.*
Nietzsche — Judgement:
The scale itself is the lie: "virtue" as a fixed weight presupposes one table of values hovering above all men, when every act of valuation is the deed of a particular kind of life asserting itself against necessity.

The hungry man does not consult a tablet of commandments — he obeys the child's hunger as his own life's hunger, and in that obedience there is more health, more instinct, more *yes* to life than in a merchant who steals to multiply what he already has. The glutton's theft is reactive, ressentiment dressed as appetite — he takes because lack gnaws at a soul already impoverished. The father's theft is a discharge of strength in service of a bond he did not choose and cannot betray. Morality that cannot tell a wolf feeding cubs from a wolf feeding vanity has already died of its own abstraction.

Judge the doer, never the deed in isolation: the same theft is noble in one hand and base in the other.

*There is no crime, only the strength or poverty of soul that commits it.*
Emerson — Judgement:
The law that punishes theft asks only what was taken; it never asks what the thief was for. But virtue is not a ledger of objects — it is the state of a man's will, and the will of the starving father bends toward his child's life, while the will of the glutton bends toward his own excess.

Compensation teaches that every act returns its true nature to the actor, not the fiction assigned by statute. The lord's rice, hoarded past use while a child starves, is already stolen from Nature's compensation — the thief who takes it back only completes a transaction the lord had corrupted. Self-reliance means each soul answers to the eternal law within, not to the granary's lock; the man who steals from need obeys that law more nearly than the one who merely obeys the statute.

They are not the same theft, and no court that weighs bushels can tell you why.

*The law counts the grain; the soul counts the reason, and only one of these is ever really weighed.*
Thomas Paine — Judgement:
The scale itself is the lord's invention. He who counts grains counted as property what nature gave in common; the "theft" begins with him, not with the starving man who reclaims a portion of the earth he was born equally entitled to.

Virtue is not a residue clinging to the act of taking, but a measure of the relation between men. A father who steals bread to keep his child alive is obeying the first and most sacred of the natural rights—self-preservation and the preservation of those depending on him—while a man who steals from surplus to feed avarice tramples on another's right for no necessity at all. To weigh these on the same scale is to mistake the letter of property for the substance of justice.

The starving man commits no crime; the law that would starve him first, and punish him second, is the true offender.

*Necessity is nature's plea, and no tribunal above nature has the right to refuse it.*
Keynes — Judgement:
The moral calculus here is not a question of natural law but of the propensities that animate men — and propensities are always mixed motives dressed as single acts.

The theft is one act, but it carries two entirely different marginal utilities: the starving man converts stolen rice into the preservation of life itself, the highest possible return on any transaction; the greedy man converts it merely into surplus accumulation, a hoarding impulse I have always regarded as economically and morally sterile. Virtue, like investment, cannot be judged by the transaction alone but by what it *does* — by its effect on aggregate welfare, not by the sanctity of the granary's title deed. A society that punishes both equally has confused property with justice, and law with morality.

The two thefts are not equal: one serves the propensity to consume for survival, the other the propensity to hoard beyond need, and only a barbarous legalism scores them the same.

*In the long run we are all judged not by what we took, but by what we needed.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
Necessity and virtue are not so easily severed as lawyers imagine. When a man steals to keep his child from wasting, he does not defy the moral law — he answers a prior and more binding one, for the right to subsist precedes every ceremony of property. The lord who hoards grain while children starve has already broken the tacit compact that makes his ownership legitimate; he has forfeited the claim he asks the law to enforce. Greed's theft multiplies suffering to gratify appetite already sated; necessity's theft merely restores the balance that unjust accumulation upset. I will not pretend these acts occupy the same moral register merely because both are called theft — that is indolence dressed as impartiality. The law that cannot distinguish a mother's hunger from a glutton's want has abdicated reason for mere mechanism.

**Verdict:** The theft born of necessity is not vice but the assertion of a right no statute may justly cancel, while theft born of greed remains true injustice.

*A law blind to hunger is not justice but tyranny wearing justice's mask.*
Hume — Judgement:
The scale of virtue is not a scale at all, but a mirror we hold up to our own passions, and we read into the act whatever sentiment it stirs in us.

An action has no intrinsic moral colour visible to reason alone; it borrows its colour entirely from the motive that animates it, and from the sympathy a spectator feels for those affected. When I regard the starving man, my imagination runs to the child's hunger, and my heart is moved to approve what my reason, examining bare property rights, cannot condone. The lord's steward, regarding only the broken lock, feels no such sympathy and calls it theft plainly. Both are true reports of sentiment; neither is a discovery about the rice.

The theft is one fact, but virtue and vice are not facts about the rice — they are facts about the sentiments of those who behold it, and by that only true measure, hunger's theft and greed's theft do not weigh the same.

*We do not discover vice in the act, but feel it in ourselves — and a father's desperation moves the human breast where a glutton's greed offends it.*
